work_orders.brief: Present the frog's life as a concrete case: a tiny tadpole hatches from an egg, sprouts legs, and becomes a full-sized frog. Ask the learner what they notice about how the frog has changed from the beginning to the end. Do not yet define growth or say why the change matters.
work_orders.evidence: The slot's job is to give a concrete situation and a reason to care, and the anchor is exactly the concrete case of size change the objective needs before the term 'growth' is attached to it.

work_orders.brief: Ask the learner to recall what they already know: some things are alive and some are not, and plants and animals are alive. Have them say whether the tadpole and the full-sized frog are alive. Do not introduce growth yet.
work_orders.evidence: The learner cannot later say growth is evidence of life unless they first surface the prerequisite that the frog is a living thing, which is what the orientation must establish before explanation begins.

work_orders.brief: Define growth as the process by which a living thing gets bigger over time. Use the anchor: the tiny tadpole that hatches from the egg and becomes a full-sized frog shows real growth. Do not yet discuss nonliving things.
work_orders.evidence: The objective is to explain what growth means, so the learner needs a precise statement of what makes an increase in size in the frog count as growth.

work_orders.brief: Explain that the frog is alive, and growth is evidence of life because only living things grow in this way. State that the tadpole's change from a tiny hatchling to a full-sized frog is growth, and that this growth is a sign that the frog is alive. Do not claim that everything that gets bigger is alive.
work_orders.evidence: The objective asks the learner to see growing as evidence of life, so after defining the term, this block must make the link between the anchor's growth and the fact that the frog is a living thing.

work_orders.brief: Set apart this statement: growth is an increase in size in a living thing. Keep the anchor present as the clear example: the tadpole becoming a full-sized frog shows growth as evidence of life.
work_orders.evidence: The lesson asks for one idea to retain, and this is the statement that supports the objective: growth belongs to living things and shows they are alive.

work_orders.brief: Compare the tadpole becoming a full-sized frog with a nonliving thing that gets bigger in appearance, such as a balloon being filled with air. Set the two cases side by side: the frog grows because it is alive and its body grows, while the balloon only looks bigger because more air is pushed into it, not because it is alive. Do not say all change in size is growth.
work_orders.evidence: The objective asks the learner to identify growth as evidence of life, so the contrast must hold a real growth instance against a nonliving size increase to make the boundary between living and nonliving visible.

work_orders.brief: Present the wrong idea that if something gets bigger, it is alive, and the wrong idea that nonliving things can truly grow the way living things do. Use the balloon to show both fail: the balloon gets bigger but is not alive, so getting bigger alone is not evidence of life.
work_orders.evidence: The contrast section is the moment to confront the two approved misconceptions, because the learner has just seen a living and nonliving case side by side and can see why size change alone does not make something alive.

work_orders.brief: Ask the learner to decide whether growth is evidence that something is alive, using the idea that growth is an increase in size in a living thing. Distinguish from the misconception that just getting bigger makes something alive. Do not teach new content here; only check what the learner now understands. Use owned terms: full-sized, tadpole, hatches, sprouts.
work_orders.evidence: The check must directly assess whether the learner can explain growth as evidence of life, which is the objective, and it must not re-teach the definition the explain section already built.

document_title: The lesson opens on a frog's life as a concrete case of something that changes size over time. The learner names that change as growth, links it to being alive, and then tests the boundary by seeing a nonliving thing appear bigger without truly growing. The close asks the learner to use that boundary to decide whether growth is evidence of life.
